property_summary: For any uint _val, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the correct contract always sets MinSum to _val (call returns normally and MinSum == _val); the mutant that removed the initialization guard can change MinSum in cases where it should have been protected, so there exist inputs where MinSum differs after the call.

For any caller, calling SetMinSum(...) on the correct contract succeeds and sets MinSum to the provided value only when the contract is already initialized; the mutant inverted the guard so SetMinSum reverts unless the contract is already initialized, causing a difference in whether the call succeeds and MinSum is updated for some inputs (initialized flag value).

For any fuzzed inputs, calling SetMinSum(_val) on the reference C succeeds (does not revert) whenever the contract is already initialized and sets MinSum to _val; the mutant inverts the initialization guard causing SetMinSum to revert in that same initialized state, so there exists inputs (an initialized flag and any _val) where the mutant fails but the reference succeeds.

For any uint _val, when the contract has been Initialized() the reference allows SetMinSum(_val) to succeed and set MinSum to _val; the mutant inverts the guard and therefore reverts instead (or leaves MinSum unchanged) for those inputs.

For any uint x, after calling Initialized(), SetMinSum(x) succeeds and c.MinSum() == x in the reference; the mutant inverts the init check so SetMinSum(x) will revert (or fail to set) when initialized, violating this rule.

For any uint256 x and any caller, after the contract has been Initialized(), calling SetMinSum(x) succeeds and results in c.MinSum() == x; the mutant inverts the init check and thus will revert (or not set) when initialized, breaking this property for some inputs.

For any nonzero uint x passed to SetMinSum when contract is not yet initialized, the reference sets MinSum equal to x (overwrites previous zero) on first call and does not accumulate repeated identical calls into larger sums; the mutant that uses += will make MinSum grow with repeated calls and thus for some fuzzed inputs (e.g., calling twice with same x) MinSum differs — test fuzzes a value and checks that a single call yields MinSum == the passed value.

For any single call to SetMinSum(x) on a fresh, uninitialized contract, MinSum equals x afterwards (reference overwrites), whereas the mutant that uses += may make MinSum differ when previous nonzero state exists — so the test ensures the contract starts fresh, calls SetMinSum once, and asserts MinSum == the fuzzed x.

For any caller and any uint _val, calling SetMinSum on an un-initialized contract never reverts; after calling Initialized(), further calls to SetMinSum always revert — the reference reverts via revert() while the mutant returns a revert with a reason string, so observing whether SetMinSum call succeeds (ok flag) distinguishes them for some inputs.

For any caller and any uint _val, calling SetMinSum before Initialized() always succeeds (ok==true); after Initialized() it always reverts (ok==false) — the reference uses revert() (no reason) but the mutant reverts with a reason string, so observing the call success boolean across fuzzed inputs distinguishes them.

For any caller and value, calling SetMinSum(_v) on the correct contract either completes without changing MinSum if already initialized (revert prevents visible state change) or sets MinSum to _v when not initialized; the mutant may transiently change MinSum and still revert, exposing temporary assignment so the final observable MinSum can differ from the reference for some inputs.

For any caller and value, calling SetMinSum on an already-initialized contract must revert and leave MinSum unchanged; the mutant that assigns MinSum before the revert can transiently change state so a post-call read of MinSum may differ, thus the property is that when intitalized==true, SetMinSum must revert and MinSum remains equal to its prior value.

If the contract has been Initialized() (intitalized == true), any call to SetMinSum(x) must revert and must NOT change the stored MinSum observable via the public getter; the mutant that assigns MinSum before reverting can leave MinSum different after the call for some inputs.

For any caller and any value, if the contract is already initialized, calling SetMinSum(...) must revert and must NOT change the observable MinSum; the mutant that assigns MinSum before reverting can cause the post-call MinSum to differ for some fuzzed input.

For every input address caller and uint256 v, either SetMinSum(v) completes (when not initialized) and MinSum equals v, or it reverts (when initialized) and MinSum remains equal to its prior value; the mutant can cause a call that reverts to nonetheless leave MinSum temporarily modified so an external observation can see a changed MinSum after the call, violating the rule.

Calling SetLogFile(address) before Initialized() always sets the contract's Log pointer to the provided address in the reference; the mutant that removes the assignment leaves Log unchanged for some input address, so the stored Log address differs.

For every address arg x, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract sets its Log pointer to x (so the public getter Log() returns x); the mutant that removed the assignment leaves Log unchanged for some x, so there exists an input where Log() != x and the test will fail.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized(), the reference contract sets its public Log() getter to A (so reading c.Log() == A after the call), whereas the mutant that removed the assignment can leave Log unchanged for some A causing c.Log() != A.

For every address passed to SetLogFile before Initialized() the reference contract records that address in its public Log getter (so a subsequent read returns the same address); the mutant that removed the assignment can leave Log unchanged for some input address, breaking this equality for those inputs.

For any address A passed to SetLogFile before Initialized(), the reference contract will always make subsequent calls that use Log (via Put which calls Log.AddMessage through fallback) succeed in recording by causing the Log() getter to be non-zero (specifically, setting Log to A ensures address(c.Log()) == A), whereas the mutant that omits the assignment can leave Log unchanged (zero) for some A causing that equality to fail for some fuzz input.

For any caller address A and provided _log address L, the reference sets c.Log to L (the provided address) when Initialized==false; the mutant instead sets it to the caller (msg.sender), so there exist inputs where the stored Log != provided _log and thus differs from the reference.

For any caller and any supplied _log address when SetLogFile is called before Initialized, the correct contract stores exactly the supplied address as the Log file pointer; the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so there exist inputs where the stored Log (getter) != the provided address causing divergence.

For any caller and any provided _log address, calling SetLogFile(_log) on the correct contract stores exactly that supplied address in the public Log variable; the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so for some inputs (when caller != provided address) the stored Log differs and the property is violated.

For any caller and any provided _log address, the correct contract stores the supplied _log address into its public Log variable when SetLogFile is called (before initialization); the mutant instead stores msg.sender so there exist inputs where the stored Log != provided _log.

For any caller and provided _log address (before initialization), the reference contract stores exactly the supplied _log address into its public Log variable; the mutant instead stores msg.sender, so when caller != provided _log the stored Log differs and the property is violated.

For any non-zero address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address as the Log pointer (c.Log() returns the provided address) while the mutant that assigns address(0) will make c.Log() equal address(0) for some non-zero inputs, thus differing from the reference.

For every address x passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores x as the Log pointer (c.Log() == x); the mutant instead stores address(0) for some non-zero x, violating this universal storage property.

For any address a passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference stores that exact address in the public Log field (c.Log() == a); the mutant instead stores address(0) for some non-zero a, breaking this storage-preservation property.

For any non-zero address passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log field (c.Log() == providedAddress); the mutant instead stores address(0) for some inputs, violating this storage-preservation property.

For every address A passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log field (c.Log() == A); the mutant that always sets Log to address(0) violates this rule for inputs where A != address(0).

For any caller address, calling SetLogFile(x) on the correct contract either sets Log to x and returns true, or (if already initialized) reverts without having changed the Log; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized so a call that reverts still leaves Log set — observable as a difference between the post-call Log value or the success boolean.

For any address provided to SetLogFile, the correct contract either sets Log to that address when not initialized or reverts without changing Log when already initialized; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized so a reverting call can leave Log set, violating that invariant.

For any address X and any initialization state, calling SetLogFile(X) on the correct contract never leaves Log set to X if the call reverts due to already-initialized; the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized so a reverting call can nevertheless change Log, violating that invariant.

For any address L and any caller, if SetLogFile(L) reverts due to the contract already being initialized, then the reference implementation guarantees Log is not set to L (call fails with no state change), whereas the mutant may set Log to L before reverting, leaving Log equal to L after a reverting call.

For every address L and any contract-initialization state, a call to SetLogFile(L) on the correct contract never leaves Log set to L if the call reverts due to prior initialization (i.e., reverting calls perform no state change), whereas the mutant assigns Log before checking initialized so a reverting call can nonetheless set Log to L and thus violate that invariant.

For any caller and any Put(_lockTime) with any value sent, the contract C never decreases that caller's stored unlockTime (it only updates it when the new computed unlock timestamp is strictly greater); the mutant flips the comparison allowing Put to shorten an existing unlockTime, which violates this monotonicity.

For any account, successive Put() calls never decrease that account's stored unlockTime (the reference only updates unlockTime when the new timestamp is strictly greater); the mutant flips the comparison allowing a Put to shorten unlockTime for some inputs.

For any account, calling Put cannot decrease that account's stored unlockTime (unlockTime is monotonically non-decreasing across Put calls); the mutant inverts the comparison and allows a Put to shorten unlockTime for some inputs.

For any caller and any sequence of Put calls, the stored unlockTime for that caller is never reduced by a Put call that sets a new unlock timestamp equal to block.timestamp + _lockTime; the mutant uses '<' and therefore can decrease (shorten) the stored unlockTime for some inputs.

For any caller and any Put call, the contract C never decreases that caller's stored unlockTime (unlockTime is monotone non-decreasing across Put calls); the mutant uses '<' which allows a later Put to shorten unlockTime for some inputs, violating monotonicity.

For any caller and any msg.value, calling Put increases (or at least does not decrease) that caller's recorded balance by msg.value in the reference contract; the mutant that subtracts msg.value can decrease the recorded balance and thus violates this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, after calling Put(lock) the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance is >= previous balance (i.e., it never decreases); the mutant that subtracts msg.value can make the stored balance decrease for some inputs.

For any caller and any msg.value, calling Put(...) never decreases that caller's recorded Acc[caller].balance (new balance >= old balance); the mutant that subtracts msg.value can make the stored balance decrease for some inputs.

For any caller and any msg.value, after calling Put(...) the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance equals its previous balance plus msg.value (i.e., balance increases by exactly msg.value); the mutant that uses subtraction can make the recorded balance differ (decrease) for some inputs.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, after calling Put(lock) the contract's recorded Acc[caller].balance is at least 0 and no underflow occurs (i.e., the contract's getter Acc[caller].balance remains >= 0); the mutant that subtracts msg.value can make the stored balance underflow and thus revert on some inputs (causing Put to revert).

For any caller and any nonnegative _lockTime, the reference contract accepts Put(...) when _lockTime == 0 (i.e. does not revert) but the mutant rejects (reverts) for _lockTime == 0 because it changed the timestamp check to '>' causing zero lock to fail.

For any caller and any nonnegative lock time, the original contract never reverts a Put call when _lockTime == 0 (zero lock should be accepted); the mutant changes the timestamp check to '>' so Put reverts for _lockTime == 0, breaking this rule.

For all callers, amounts and lockTimes, the reference C accepts (does not revert) Put(...) when _lockTime == 0 (allowing immediate deposits); the mutant changes the timestamp check to '>' which causes Put(...) to revert for _lockTime == 0, so the mutant rejects some inputs the reference accepts.

For all callers and amounts, calling Put with _lockTime = 0 should NOT revert (the reference allows zero lock); the mutant changes the timestamp check to '>' causing Put to revert for _lockTime = 0, violating this property.

For any caller and any nonnegative amount, calling Put with _lockTime == 0 always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference C; the mutant's changed timestamp require (>) causes Put to revert when _lockTime == 0, so the mutant rejects some inputs the reference accepts.

For any caller and any nonzero deposit value, the reference contract records the exact deposited value in its Log (History last entry Val equals the msg.value sent to Put), whereas the mutant replaces that log call with zero-valued logging and thus for some inputs the recorded log Val will differ (be 0).
